introduction: “Religions are many, but the reality of religion is one.” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá said it in churches, synagogues and lecture halls across the West, and Bahá’u’lláh had written it before him: the systems of belief are rays of one light, their differences belong to the ages in which they appeared and to what followers have added, and a religion that causes hatred has lost its reason to exist. A hundred of the guide’s three hundred quotations are given here, ten from each tenth of its length. Beside them stand a hundred voices from elsewhere. Many have said something like it: the Rig Veda, Amos, Malachi, the Qur’an, Justin Martyr, Symmachus, Rúmí, Kabir, Blake, William James. About one in four pushes back and ends in a question. Chesterton holds that the religions differ most in what they teach; the Gospels and the Qur’an have their exclusive verses; Gandhi and Vivekananda want harmony without merging; Madison trusts many sects more than one faith; Feuerbach and Paine take the argument somewhere else entirely.
questions: Bahá’u’lláh attributes the differences between religions to the needs of their ages and to human additions. Chesterton says they differ most in what they teach. Take two religions you know something of: which account fits better?
“No man cometh unto the Father, but by me”; “none other name”; “other than the Surrender”. How do the readings ask a Christian or a Muslim to hear such verses, and what would be lost or kept?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes the rivers will merge in one sea; Vivekananda and Gandhi want each faith to grow by its own law. What is the difference between unity and uniformity in religion?
If religion causes hatred, “irreligion is better”. Marx, Paine and Jefferson each drew a conclusion from religion’s record. Where do the readings part company with them?

The Prophets were united and their followers are in strife. Paul saw parties in his own churches, and Dostoevsky imagined a church that no longer wanted its founder. What turns a founder’s teaching into a cause of division?

Madison thought freedom safest among many sects, and the Qur’an says God chose not to make mankind one community. What would a single common faith need in order not to become a single common pressure?

outside.why: The peoples “derive their inspiration from one heavenly Source”; their ordinances differ with the needs of their ages. The Qur’an: for each We have appointed a divine law and a traced-out way.
All are “the subjects of one God”. Amos has God say it to Israel’s face: are ye not as children of the Ethiopians unto me? Did I not bring the Philistines from Caphtor, as I brought you from Egypt?

Bahá’u’lláh puts the differences between religions down to the requirements of their ages. Chesterton thought the popular version of this false: the religions differ little in rites and greatly in what they teach. What are the largest differences in teaching, and how do the readings account for them?
“Love ye all religions … and show that love through deeds and not through the tongue.” John: let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.
“It is not necessary to lower Abraham to raise Jesus.” The Qur’an’s creed: we make no distinction between any of His messengers.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá will not rank the Messengers against each other. Paul: there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. How do the readings understand a claim like this without lowering it?
The systems of religion “have proceeded from one Source, and are the rays of one Light”. Rúmí: the lamps are different, but the Light is the same.
One source, many forms. The Rig Veda, three thousand years ago: to what is One, sages give many a title.
Religion is meant for unity; “make it not the cause of dissension and strife”. Swift: we have just enough religion to make us hate, but not enough to make us love one another.
“If religion become the cause of enmity, it is the very essence of evil.” Pascal, a believer: men never do evil so completely and cheerfully as when they do it from religious conviction.

If the remedy becomes the cause of sickness, “to abandon it is preferable”. Marx went on from there: religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature, the opium of the people. Is the test ‘Abdu’l-Bahá proposes one that Marx could accept?
The teachings say people “should see any shortcomings in themselves, not in others”. Jesus: first cast out the beam out of thine own eye.
The systems of belief “should never be allowed to foster the feelings of animosity among men”. Ashoka’s rock edict: whoever condemns other religions harms his own.
“The religion of God is one … but still, it needs must be made new.” Hebrews: that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away.

Religion must be made new. Jesus observed what stands in the way: no man having drunk old wine straightway desireth new, for he saith, The old is better. What is it in religion that people cannot bear to see renewed?
“Spring returneth over and over again.” The Song of Solomon: lo, the winter is past; the flowers appear on the earth.
The dispensations are “one and the same”, returning like spring. The Preacher says of all things that what has been is what shall be. Is the renewal of religion a return or an advance?
“The teachings of Christ have been promulgated by Bahá’u’lláh”, with new teachings for present conditions. Jesus on his own relation to Moses: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
All the Manifestations summoned mankind “anew to the fundamental oneness of God”. The summons in its oldest surviving form: Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God is one Lord.
They were iconoclasts, uprooting false beliefs. A Greek philosopher did the same to Homer’s gods: one god, the greatest, in no way like mortals in body or in thought.
The Manifestations destroyed false religious beliefs. The first commandment: thou shalt have no other gods before me. How does a religion that began by breaking idols come to honour other religions?
What was “revealed unto the Prophets of old” is given again in brief. The Qur’an: He hath ordained for you that religion which He commended unto Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus.
“This is the changeless Faith of God, eternal in the past, eternal in the future.” The Qur’an’s profession: we believe in that which was revealed unto Abraham, Moses, Jesus and the prophets.
The Prophets appear “clothed in divers attire”, proclaiming the same Faith. Hebrews: God at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past by the prophets.
All the Prophets, says Bahá’u’lláh, abide in the same tabernacle and utter the same speech. Jesus in John’s Gospel: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me. How do the readings hear that sentence?

The ordinances “were completed through that which was revealed in the Qur’an to the Seal of the Prophets”. Each of the older faiths has a verse of this kind. What does completion mean in a religion that also expects renewal?
He has appeared with “the testimony of Moses … and the proofs of all the Prophets”. Moses had told his people to expect another: a Prophet like unto thee.

“The Sun of Divinity … has revealed itself in various mirrors. Though these mirrors are many, yet the Sun is one.” Shelley: life, like a dome of many-coloured glass, stains the white radiance of eternity.
Many mirrors, one sun. Tennyson: our little systems are but broken lights of thee, and thou, O Lord, art more than they.
“Religions are many, but the reality of religion is one … Reality is one.” Paul’s rule for finding it: prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
“Man must be a lover of the light, no matter from what dayspring it may appear.” Justin, a Christian of the second century, counted Socrates among his own: those who lived reasonably are Christians.
“Attachment to the lantern is not loving the light.” John’s prologue: the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world.

A seeker of truth, “no matter from what source it come”. The Buddha’s blind men each took hold of one part of an elephant and came to blows over what it was like. Does everyone hold a part, and how would one ever know the whole?
May “these many rivers, each flowing along in diverse and separated beds … find their way back to the circumambient sea”. The Chandogya Upanishad’s image is the same: rivers that become the sea.

The rivers are to “merge together and rise up in a single wave”. Vivekananda told the Parliament of Religions in 1893 that the Christian is not to become a Hindu nor the Hindu a Christian; each must grow by his own law. Is unity a merging, or a harmony of things that stay distinct?

The old instruments are out of tune, and Bahá’u’lláh brought a new one that “includes all notes”. Gandhi: the need of the moment is not one religion, but mutual respect; not the dead level, but unity in diversity. Does a new instrument replace the old ones?

“The fundamentals of the religion of God are … one in reality.” The last great pagan senator, pleading before a Christian emperor: we look on the same stars; we cannot attain to so great a secret by one road.
“The Books of God have been revealed for the upbuilding of fellowship and union.” Malachi: have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?

“We must investigate reality … If the nations of the world investigate reality, they will agree.” Milton trusted the same process: let Truth and Falsehood grapple; who ever knew Truth put to the worse in a free and open encounter?

Investigation will unite the nations. Mill valued investigation for the opposite result, a lasting diversity of opinion that keeps each side honest. Has free inquiry tended to unite people, or to multiply their views?

Investigate the foundations and “we discover much ground for agreement”. William James, after surveying the world’s religious experience: the warring gods and formulas cancel each other, but there is a certain uniform deliverance in which religions all appear to meet.
Division comes from “imitations of forms and ancestral beliefs”. The Qur’an: they say, we follow that wherein we found our fathers.
Differences “only result from their attachment to prejudice”. Bacon on why minds do not simply see: the human understanding is no dry light; what a man had rather were true he more readily believes.

“The differences among the religions of the world are due to the varying types of minds.” Blake said nearly that in 1788: the religions of all nations are derived from each nation’s different reception.
Different minds, different religions. Xenophanes: if oxen and horses had hands, horses would draw the forms of gods like horses.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá traces the differences of religion to the variety of human minds and still holds their source to be one. Feuerbach took the first step and stopped: the true sense of theology is anthropology. What keeps the first claim from collapsing into the second?
“So shall we see the truth in all religions, for truth is in all and truth is one!” Kabir has God say: I am neither in temple nor in mosque; I am beside thee.
“Each Prophet fulfilled the promise of the One Who came before Him and, likewise, Each announced the One Who would follow.” In the Qur’an Jesus does both in one sentence.

The Founders “are one in spirit and reality”. Boccaccio’s three rings are so alike that the father himself could hardly tell the true one, and the question remains pending. Is that the same thought, or a sceptic’s version of it?
“All breathe the same atmosphere, live upon the same earth, move beneath the same heavens.” An American president in 1963: we all inhabit this small planet; we all breathe the same air.
All are servants of one God. Malachi: from the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles.
“The fundamental truth of the Manifestations is peace.” Micah: nation shall not lift up a sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
“Each of the holy Manifestations announced the glad tidings of His successor.” Jesus at the last supper: he shall give you another Comforter.
The sacred Books were written for love, “and yet … we have the sad spectacle of war and bloodshed”. Mark Twain made a congregation hear what its prayer for victory was asking.
The Prophets “were in the utmost unity, but Their followers are in strife”. Paul saw it begin in his own churches: I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas.

Founders united, followers at war. Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor tells the returned Christ that the church has corrected his work and does not need him. What do institutions do to what their founders brought?

We dispute “because we have shut our eyes to the underlying principle of all religions, that God is one, that He is the Father of us all”. Paul at Athens: he hath made of one blood all nations of men.
“We must lay aside all prejudice — whether it be religious, racial, political or patriotic.” Paul: there is neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female.

All prejudice is to be laid aside. Burke defended it by name: we cherish our old prejudices, and the longer they have lasted the more we cherish them. Is there any inherited attachment that is not a prejudice?
The variance of religions is “adherence to forms and imitations which have arisen”. Isaiah: their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men.
“The clouds and mists of imitations have obscured the Sun of Truth.” Jesus: ye lay aside the commandment of God and hold the tradition of men.
When the mists of superstition disperse, “all will see the Sun aright and alike”. Plato’s prisoners take shadows for the truth until one of them is turned towards the light.

We have imagined it a religious duty to “shun each other and consider each other contaminated”. Peter needed a vision to unlearn it: God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.
“Anathema and execration were utterly abrogated.” The Qur’an had already forbidden one form of it: revile not those unto whom they pray beside God.
No one is to consider another “as bad”. The Qur’an: say not unto one who offereth you peace, Thou art not a believer.

Religion must be the cause of fellowship or it “has no necessity for the human world”. Paine concluded that it had none: I do not believe in the creed professed by any church; my own mind is my own church. What does the independent search for truth find that Paine did not?

If religion becomes a cause of hatred “it were better that it should not exist”. Jefferson’s remedy was to make it harmless in law: it does me no injury for my neighbour to say there are twenty gods, or no god. Is a religion that injures no one the same as one that brings joy?
The sovereign remedy is “the union of all its peoples in one universal Cause, one common Faith”. Paul: one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.

Bahá’u’lláh names one common Faith as the remedy. The Qur’an says God could have made mankind one community and chose not to, that He may try each by what He gave: so vie one with another in good works. Is the variety of religions a sickness to be healed, or part of a design?
One universal Cause for all peoples. Madison held that freedom of conscience is safest where sects are many and none can dominate. What would protect the dissenter in a world of one faith?
“May you view mankind as the sheep of God and know for a certainty that He is the real Shepherd.” Jesus: other sheep I have, which are not of this fold; there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.
“Consider how the religions of God served the world of humanity!” Jesus’ test: by their fruits ye shall know them.

Each religion is credited with raising and uniting a people. Gibbon tells the rise of Christianity as a historian and ends it on the ruins of the Capitol. Can the same history be told as progress and as decline?
In Persia “the various religionists … have united in complete fellowship and love”. What pagans said of the first Christians: see how they love one another.
At their meetings “you cannot say who is a Jew, who is a Muslim, who is a Parsi or who is a Christian”. Ibn ‘Arabí: my heart has become capable of every form.
Muslims, Buddhists, Jews, Christians and Zoroastrians meet as one. The tenth Sikh Guru: the temple and the mosque are the same; all men are the same.
All peoples and religions “beneath one tent”. Ruth crossing from one people and one worship to another: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.
People from all religions have entered. Jesus: many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob.
“Religious tolerance of this kind would have been hitherto impossible.” Locke, in 1689, asked only that no one be shut out of civil rights for his religion, and was thought radical.
“As Christians believe in Moses, so the Jews should believe in Jesus.” Jesus had argued the same connection: had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me.

All should “become … believers in all the Prophets. Then all disputes would” end. The Qur’an’s short chapter to those who would not: unto you your religion, and unto me my religion. Is agreeing to differ a failure of unity or a form of it?
The difference between the religions “is one of terminology only”. Juliet: that which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet.
“When Christians act according to the teachings of Christ, they are called Bahá’ís.” Jesus put the name below the deed: not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord.

The foundations are one and only the terms differ. Peter: there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved. Can a name matter that much and the difference still be one of terminology?

That the foundation of all religions is one is called a teaching “new and specialized to this Manifestation”. Gibbon says the Roman magistrate thought all religions equally useful, the philosopher equally false, the people equally true. What is new here that Rome did not have?
The oneness of the Holy Manifestations was heard “with the utmost joy”. Whitman claimed them all: my faith is the greatest of faiths and the least of faiths, enclosing worship ancient and modern.
“In all churches and mosques there is the remembrance of God.” The Qur’an defends cloisters, churches, oratories and mosques together, “wherein the name of God is oft mentioned”.
“All peoples worship one God; none worship Satan.” Pope’s Universal Prayer: Father of all, in every age, in every clime adored.
A confederation of religions, its influence reaching the world. Rabbi Heschel, half a century later: no religion is an island; we are all involved with one another.
A world conference of religions might “abandon all those doctrines which are mere dogmas and traditions”. Kant’s motto for such work: have courage to use your own understanding.
They would “retain only what is absolute and fundamental”. William Penn had named it: the humble, meek, merciful, just, pious and devout souls are everywhere of one religion.
Material civilization joined with divine civilization: the man of intellect with the man of spiritual capacity. Tennyson: let knowledge grow from more to more, but more of reverence in us dwell.
“The Bahá’ís are the friends of all religions.” The Qur’an to Muslims about Jews and Christians: say, our God and your God is One.

No one is any longer “defined by such labels as Jewish or Christian”. Micah’s vision of peace keeps the labels: all people will walk every one in the name of his god, and we will walk in the name of the Lord. Do the names have to go for the conflict to end?
The Bahá’ís “believe in the fundamental truth of all the religions”. The Qur’an on Jews, Christians and Sabaeans: whoever believeth and doeth right, no fear shall come upon them.
Reality is love, knowledge, justice, fellowship; “all divine Prophets established and promoted this”. Micah’s summary: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with thy God.

Whoever serves God “is a follower of all the teachings of the Divine prophets”. The Qur’an says no religion but the Surrender will be accepted, and calls Abraham and Jesus’ disciples surrendered ones. Is that verse a wall or a wide door?
“We must visualize the Universal harmony of religions.” Tolstoy’s bishop, having tried to teach three old hermits the Lord’s Prayer, sees them run to him across the water and bows to them.
The hope “that all religion become one … and all nations as one”. Isaiah says it of Israel’s two great enemies: blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands.
“The day … of a universal language and of the union of all religions.” Zamenhof invented a language for that day.

malachi-in-every-place-incense.text: For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered unto my name, and a pure offering: for my name shall be great among the heathen, saith the Lord of hosts

john-lighteth-every-man.text: That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world

matthew-from-the-east-and-west.text: And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven

amos-children-of-the-ethiopians.text: Are ye not as children of the Ethiopians unto me, O children of Israel? saith the Lord. Have not I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir

isaiah-blessed-be-egypt.text: In that day shall Israel be the third with Egypt and with Assyria, even a blessing in the midst of the land: Whom the Lord of hosts shall bless, saying, Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance

micah-every-one-in-the-name-of-his-god.text: For all people will walk every one in the name of his god, and we will walk in the name of the Lord our God for ever and ever

quran-religion-commended-to-noah.text: He hath ordained for you that religion which He commended unto Noah, and that which We inspire in thee (Muhammad), and that which We commended unto Abraham and Moses and Jesus, saying: Establish the religion, and be not divided therein. Dreadful for the idolaters is that unto which thou callest them. Allah chooseth for Himself whom He will, and guideth unto Himself him who turneth (toward Him).

quran-other-than-the-surrender.text: And whoso seeketh as religion other than the Surrender (to Allah) it will not be accepted from him, and he will be a loser in the Hereafter.

quran-a-law-and-a-way.text: And unto thee have We revealed the Scripture with the truth, confirming whatever Scripture was before it, and a watcher over it. So judge between them by that which Allah hath revealed, and follow not their desires away from the truth which hath come unto thee. For each We have appointed a divine law and a traced-out way. Had Allah willed He could have made you one community. But that He may try you by that which He hath given you (He hath made you as ye are). So vie one with another in good works. Unto Allah ye will all return, and He will then inform you of that wherein ye differ.

quran-sacred-rites-for-each-nation.text: Unto each nation have We given sacred rites which they are to perform; so let them not dispute with thee of the matter, but summon thou unto thy Lord. Lo! thou indeed followest right guidance.

quran-revealed-unto-abraham.text: Say (O Muslims): We believe in Allah and that which is revealed unto us and that which was revealed unto Abraham, and Ishmael, and Isaac, and Jacob, and the tribes, and that which Moses and Jesus received, and that which the prophets received from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and unto Him we have surrendered.

quran-your-religion-and-mine.text: Say: O disbelievers! I worship not that which ye worship; Nor worship ye that which I worship. And I shall not worship that which ye worship. Nor will ye worship that which I worship. Unto you your religion, and unto me my religion

pope-jehovah-jove-or-lord.text: Father of all! in ev'ry age, / In ev'ry clime ador'd, / By saint, by savage, and by sage, / Jehovah, Jove, or Lord
pope-jehovah-jove-or-lord.author: Alexander Pope

blake-all-religions-are-one.text: The Religions of all Nations are derived from each Nation's different reception of the Poetic Genius
blake-all-religions-are-one.author: William Blake

whitman-greatest-of-faiths-and-least.text: I do not despise you priests, all time, the world over, / My faith is the greatest of faiths and the least of faiths, / Enclosing worship ancient and modern
whitman-greatest-of-faiths-and-least.author: Walt Whitman

justin-lived-reasonably.text: We have been taught that Christ is the first-born of God, and we have declared above that He is the Word of whom every race of men were partakers; and those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists
justin-lived-reasonably.author: Justin Martyr

buddha-seeing-one-side.text: With regard to these things they're attached — some contemplatives & brahmans. They quarrel & fight — people seeing one side
buddha-seeing-one-side.locator: 6.4, the blind men and the elephant
buddha-seeing-one-side.year: c. 5th century BCE; written down later

rights.note: Modern translation, offered for free distribution; the closing verse.

chesterton-differ-in-what-they-teach.text: It is false; it is the opposite of the fact. The religions of the earth do not greatly differ in rites and forms; they do greatly differ in what they teach
chesterton-differ-in-what-they-teach.author: G. K. Chesterton

james-uniform-deliverance.text: The warring gods and formulas of the various religions do indeed cancel each other, but there is a certain uniform deliverance in which religions all appear to meet
james-uniform-deliverance.author: William James

symmachus-not-by-one-road.text: We look on the same stars, the sky is common, the same world surrounds us. What difference does it make by what pains each seeks the truth? We cannot attain to so great a secret by one road
symmachus-not-by-one-road.author: Quintus Aurelius Symmachus
symmachus-not-by-one-road.work: Memorial to the Emperor Valentinian II
